summary: An April 1 RFC and a humorous one. It claims to solve the Y10K problem, which comes from the year 10000 needing five digits instead of four, along with tongue-in-cheek variants named for hexadecimal and Roman numerals. It is informational, not a real standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke points out that four-digit years stop at 9999. It then proposes an elaborate format for dates far beyond that point.

questions: how does rfc 2550 format large years
why are carets used in rfc 2550
subtitle: An April 1st joke that invents a date format for years beyond 9999.

tldr.problem: This April 1st RFC jokes that switching from two-digit to four-digit years only postpones a date-format problem until year 10,000.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes adding letters and, for still larger years, carets and other markers to create sortable dates.
tldr.outcome: The document is satire about date formats and does not specify a real Internet standard.

today: RFC 2550 is an Informational April 1st joke RFC about extending date formats beyond four-digit years.

sections.title: The Y10K Problem
sections.content:
The memo jokes that the common Y2K fix, using four-digit years, leads to another boundary at year 10,000. It warns against assuming that software will be retired before its date format runs out.

It compares fixed-width approaches and argues that any fixed range can eventually be exceeded. The RFC is an April 1st humor document.
sections.plainLanguage: Four digits can represent years only through 9999. The joke asks what happens to software when the year needs more digits.

sections.title: A Sortable Year Format
sections.content:
For years from 10,000 through 99,999, the proposal places an “A” before the five-digit year. Later blocks use other letters, so a date's ASCII representation can be sorted lexically.

For larger ranges, the memo describes prefixes with carets and letters. It also gives a complement scheme for years before the common era and says dates are relative to International Atomic Time.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed format adds letters before longer year numbers. Its goal is for dates to stay in order when sorted as text.

sections.title: Precision and Open Issues
sections.content:
After the year, the format may include digits for month, day, hour, minute, second, and finer fractions. A date that is a prefix of another sorts before the longer date, according to the memo.

The RFC also lists unresolved issues such as comparing dates from different calendar systems and agreeing on time synchronization beyond Earth. The formalism and far-future projections carry the April 1st joke.
sections.plainLanguage: The format can add more digits for more precise times. The memo also jokes that calendars and timekeeping could become difficult on very long timescales.

references.text: Crocker, D. and P. Overell, "Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF", RFC 2234, November 1997.
